281.title: The mystics in you
281.hook: mystics aren't a different species; they paid attention for a long time
281.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians read the mystics as companions in prayer, and some practice daily periods of quiet attention, such as silent prayer, slow scripture reading, or doing ordinary work with God in mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was my joy: Seraphim of Sarov's greeting, Christ is risen. Your line was acquire peace.

When people hear the word mystic, they often picture someone floating a few inches off the floor. Glowing eyes. Visions every Tuesday. Someone simply built differently from the rest of us. But look at who you've actually met these twenty days. A soldier with a limp who cooked dinner. A dyer's daughter. A sick woman in a small room. A monk who copied books. A young man who couldn't find a minister to help him. A nun who didn't know how to begin her book. Not a different species. Ordinary people. So what made them mystics?
screen: `FLOATING OFF THE FLOOR?` → `A COOK, A DYER'S DAUGHTER.` → `NOT A DIFFERENT SPECIES.`

segments.voice: The word mystic comes from Greek. It shares a root with mystery, and goes back to a verb that means to close, the eyes or the lips. In the early church, mystical didn't mean spooky. It meant hidden: the hidden meaning inside scripture, the hidden life of God in the bread and wine, the hidden depth inside an ordinary life. A mystic, in that old sense, has learned to see what's hidden in plain sight. How did they learn? Look back. The abbas and ammas: give me a word, tend the fire, go to your cell and stay put. Gregory: always further in. Benedict: pray and work, and treat the pots like altar vessels. Hildegard saw greening. Bernard mapped four loves. Francis called the sun his brother. The Cloud: reached by love. Julian, the anchoress, saw the hazelnut and heard a love bigger than the hurt. Catherine spoke up. The Imitation: follow quietly. Teresa found a room further in; John found that dark is not absent. Brother Lawrence found God among the pots. Fox found that of God in everyone. Seraphim acquired peace. Under all of it runs one thread. They paid attention: to God, to scripture, to the people in front of them, to the ordinary thing in their hands. Not for a minute. For years. The Psalm puts it plainly: "Be still, and know that I am God." The mystics themselves said seeing God is a gift, not something anyone can earn or force. But in their stories, again and again, the door opens where someone is looking.
screen: `MYSTIC: TO CLOSE THE EYES.` · `HIDDEN IN PLAIN SIGHT.` · `TWENTY DAYS, ONE THREAD.` · `BE STILL, AND KNOW.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing in front of you, your hand, a cup, the light on the wall, and look at it as if you'd never seen it before. When the mind wanders, bring it back, like Brother Lawrence, without fuss; that small return, over and over, for years, is the thread these twenty days kept finding. If you pray, you can simply be still, and know.
Mystic. From a Greek word about closing the eyes: someone who learns to see what's hidden in plain sight.
Your line: attention is the beginning. That closes our stretch on the mystics. Tomorrow, the family of churches.

282.title: One church, then many
282.hook: for a thousand years there was broadly one church, with arguments; then came divisions
282.howItsDone: Many Christians pray each January during the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, and churches of different traditions often worship together at ecumenical services, while keeping their own practices.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was mystic, someone who learns to see what's hidden in plain sight. Your line was attention is the beginning.

Count the churches on one ordinary main street. Catholic on one corner, Baptist across the street. Methodist, Lutheran, Pentecostal, a Greek Orthodox church with a dome, a storefront with a hand-painted sign. If you didn't grow up inside one, it can be confusing. Aren't they all Christian? Why so many? It's a fair question, and Christians ask it too, sometimes with real sadness. Over the next couple of weeks you'll meet this family of churches one by one, each described the way it describes itself. Today, the family tree.
screen: `COUNT THE CHURCHES.` → `WHY SO MANY?` → `THE FAMILY TREE.`

segments.voice: For roughly the first thousand years, Christians broadly thought of themselves as one church. Not one building or one boss, but one family across the Roman world, with great centers at Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem. It was never a quiet family. There were fierce arguments, and some real early separations: after a council in 451, several ancient churches, including the Coptic, Ethiopian, Armenian and Syriac churches, did not accept its wording and parted from those who did. They're still here today. The split this path turns to next came later. Over centuries, the Greek-speaking East and the Latin-speaking West grew apart: different languages and customs, arguments over the pope's authority and over a phrase in the creed. In 1054, envoys from Rome and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated each other. The break hardened over the centuries after, into what are now the Catholic Church and the Orthodox Church. Then, in 1517, a German monk named Martin Luther posted his objections to practices in the Western church, and the Protestant Reformation began. Out of it came Lutherans, Reformed and Presbyterian churches, Anglicans, Anabaptists, and later Baptists, Methodists, Pentecostals and many more. Long before any of this, Paul used a picture Christians keep coming back to: "For as the body is one, and hath many members, and all the members of that one body, being many, are one body: so also is Christ." And: "the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee." In 1965, the pope and the patriarch of Constantinople lifted the excommunications of 1054. The divisions remain. So does the longing.
screen: `A THOUSAND YEARS, BROADLY ONE.` · `451: THE ANCIENT EASTERN CHURCHES.` · `1054: EAST AND WEST.` · `1517: THE REFORMATION.`

segments.voice: Think of one church that isn't your own, or, if you don't belong to one, a church you've driven past. Picture its doors on a Sunday morning: families, old couples, someone alone, walking in. If you pray, pray for them in whatever words come; if you don't, just wish them well, and hold them for a moment as part of one family.
One church. How Christians broadly saw themselves for a thousand years, before the divisions, and what many still long for.
Your line: one body, many parts. One very big, very complicated family. Day two hundred eighty-two, done.

283.title: The councils
283.hook: bishops met at Nicaea (325) and Chalcedon (451) to settle who Jesus is
283.tomorrow: the ancient churches of the east
283.howItsDone: Many churches, Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and others, say the Nicene Creed together at the main Sunday service, usually standing, after the readings and sermon.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was one church: a thousand years of one family, with arguments, and then the splits. Your line was one body, many parts.

The year 325, a lakeside town called Nicaea, in what is now Turkey. Bishops arrive from across the empire, some on imperial horses paid for by the emperor Constantine. Tradition says a few carry scars: not long before, Christians were being arrested and tortured, and some of these old men, the story goes, still limp from it. The emperor has called them together because the church is arguing so loudly it can be heard in the marketplace. A priest from Alexandria named Arius has been teaching that the Son of God was created, the first and greatest of all creatures, but a creature. His opponents say people are singing his ideas in catchy songs. Others are furious. So the bishops sit down in one room to answer a question that sounds simple: who is Jesus?
screen: `NICAEA, THE YEAR 325.` → `BISHOPS WITH SCARS.` → `WHO IS JESUS?`

segments.voice: A council is a gathering of church leaders to settle something together. The Greek word is synodos, a way taken together, the root of synod. The idea goes back to the Bible: in Acts 15 the apostles and elders meet in Jerusalem to argue about whether new believers must keep the Jewish law, and send out a letter that says, it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us. At Nicaea, the bishops rejected Arius. Their statement said the Son is of one being with the Father, one Greek word, homoousios. Fifty-six years later, a second council, at Constantinople, expanded it into the creed many churches still say, the Nicene Creed. In the old English of the Book of Common Prayer, the Son is "God of God, Light of Light, Very God of very God, Begotten, not made." Then in 451, at Chalcedon, a council asked the next question: if Jesus is truly God, is he truly human too? Yes: one person, two natures, not mixed and not split. The councils didn't invent faith in Jesus; they tried to put into words what churches were already praying and singing, and they argued fiercely doing it, with politics mixed in. And not everyone accepted every council. Chalcedon, especially, led to a lasting split, which is tomorrow's story. Notice how the council's creed began: not I believe, but we believe.
screen: `SYNODOS: A WAY TAKEN TOGETHER.` · `NICAEA: OF ONE BEING WITH THE FATHER.` · `CHALCEDON: TRULY GOD, TRULY HUMAN.` · `NOT EVERYONE AGREED.` · then, large: `BEGOTTEN, NOT MADE.`

segments.voice: Read the Nicene Creed once, slowly, the way you'd read a letter from someone who had suffered to write it, and notice which line stops you: the one you love, or the one you don't understand. If you pray, say it aloud; if you don't, read it as a very old answer to a very old question.

Your line: we believe. Much of a faith is handed on by the people who came before. See you tomorrow.

284.title: The ancient churches of the east
284.hook: Copts, Ethiopians, Armenians and Syriacs keep some of the oldest Christian traditions on earth
284.howItsDone: Oriental Orthodox Christians worship in ancient liturgical languages such as Coptic, Ge'ez, Armenian and Syriac, keep long fasts through the year, and many stand through services that last several hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was council: Nicaea and Chalcedon, bishops trying to say who Jesus is. Your line was we believe.

In the highlands of northern Ethiopia there's a town called Lalibela, where, many centuries ago, whole churches were carved down into the solid red rock. Not built. Carved, from the top down, like sculptures you can walk into. On a feast day before dawn, crowds in white shawls fill the trenches around them, and priests chant in Ge'ez, a language no longer spoken in daily life, kept alive in prayer. Drums. Sistrums, little metal rattles. Swaying. Christianity is often pictured in a European cathedral or an American strip-mall church. Lalibela is a reminder that very old Christian traditions are African and Asian.
screen: `LALIBELA: CHURCHES CARVED FROM ROCK.` → `CHANTING IN GE'EZ.` → `VERY OLD, AFRICAN AND ASIAN.`

segments.voice: The Oriental Orthodox churches are a family of six: the Coptic church of Egypt, the Ethiopian and Eritrean churches, the Armenian Apostolic church, the Syriac Orthodox church, and the Malankara church in India. Oriental just means eastern. Orthodox, yes, but a separate family from the Greek and Russian Orthodox you may know. Why? Remember Chalcedon, in 451: Christ in two natures. These churches didn't accept that wording. They held to an older phrase from Cyril of Alexandria: one nature of God the Word made flesh, divine and human united, never mixed and never divided. Others called them monophysites, one-nature people, a label they reject. They say miaphysite: one united nature. For centuries each side thought the other had lost something essential. Then, in the late twentieth century, theologians from these churches, the Eastern Orthodox and the Catholic Church agreed in joint statements that much of the split had been about words, and that they share far more than they thought. Armenian tradition remembers its king as the first to make Christianity a kingdom's official faith, in the early 300s. The Ethiopian church loves the story in Acts 8 of an Ethiopian official baptized on a desert road, and a line from the Psalms: "Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God." Coptic, their old church language, descends from the language of the pharaohs. Syriac is a form of Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke. These churches have lived through empires, massacres and exile, and some of their people have had to flee their homes. And every Sunday, they still sing.

segments.voice: Hold one fact: in Ethiopian Orthodox practice, a church is consecrated with a tabot, a carved tablet standing for the ark of the covenant, kept wrapped in cloth. Picture the white shawls before dawn, people keeping one way of praying for many centuries. If you pray, pray for these churches and their people far from home; if not, hold them in mind with respect.

285.title: The Church of the East
285.hook: Christians who traveled the Silk Road to China and India in the first millennium
285.howItsDone: The Assyrian Church of the East and its sister churches still pray in Syriac, keep an ancient liturgy called the Liturgy of Addai and Mari, and honor the cross without a figure on it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Oriental Orthodox: Copts, Ethiopians, Armenians, Syriacs and the Malankara church. Your line was very old, still singing.

In the 1620s, workers digging near Xi'an, in China, pulled a huge stone slab out of the ground. Taller than a man, with a cross carved at the top, rising out of a lotus flower. Below it, nearly two thousand Chinese characters, and a border of writing in Syriac. The stone had been set up in 781. It told how a monk named Alopen reached the Tang emperor's capital in 635, carrying scriptures, and how the emperor welcomed him, had the books translated, and let him build a monastery. Christians in China, in the 600s.
screen: `A STONE FROM THE YEAR 781.` → `A CROSS RISING FROM A LOTUS.` → `CHRISTIANS IN CHINA, 635.`

segments.voice: The Church of the East grew up in Persia, beyond the Roman Empire's eastern border, among Christians who prayed in Syriac, a cousin of Jesus's own Aramaic. Its leader, the catholicos, sat in Seleucia-Ctesiphon, near modern Baghdad. Outside Rome, it went its own way on the councils. Westerners long called it Nestorian, after a bishop condemned in 431, a label the church didn't choose and many today find misleading. Along the Silk Road, with its caravans, oases and monasteries, merchants and monks from this church carried the gospel across Central Asia to China, and down to India, where the Saint Thomas Christians trace their faith to the apostle Thomas himself. In China they called their faith the luminous teaching. At its height, around 1300, this one church stretched from the Mediterranean to the Pacific, with more territory than any church in Europe. A monk from near Beijing, Rabban Sauma, traveled west and met the king of France in 1287, and the pope in 1288. Then came centuries of hardship: plagues, conquests, the collapse of the Mongol empire, massacres. The church shrank almost to nothing in China and Central Asia. Its heirs today, the Assyrian Church of the East, the Ancient Church of the East, and churches in communion with Rome such as the Chaldeans, are small, many of them refugees from Iraq and Syria. In Acts, Jesus told his friends they would be his witnesses "unto the uttermost part of the earth." Most maps of Christian history draw that line going west. This church went east too, early and far.
screen: `A CHURCH BEYOND ROME, IN PERSIA.` · `A LABEL IT DIDN'T CHOOSE.` · `ALONG THE SILK ROAD TO CHINA.` · `SMALL NOW, MANY OF THEM REFUGEES.` · then, large: `UNTO THE UTTERMOST PART OF THE EARTH.`

Thousands of miles, walked by monks and merchants more than a thousand years ago. If you pray, pray for the Christians who still live along that road, and those who had to leave it; if not, let the size of the map sink in.

286.hook: East and West split, over authority and a word in the creed, with faults on both sides
286.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox leaders now meet regularly, and every year on the feasts of Saint Andrew and of Saints Peter and Paul delegations from Rome and Constantinople visit each other to pray together.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was luminous teaching: the Church of the East, monks and merchants on the Silk Road. Your line was the road went east.

July, 1054. Constantinople's great church, Hagia Sophia, during the afternoon service. Three envoys from the pope in Rome, led by a cardinal named Humbert, walk up the aisle and lay a document on the altar. It excommunicates the patriarch of Constantinople. Then they walk out, shaking the dust off their feet. A deacon runs after them, begging them to take it back. They refuse. Days later the patriarch, Michael Cerularius, excommunicates the envoys in return. The strange part: the pope who sent them had already died, so some historians wonder whether the document even counted. Nobody in that church could know what they were watching, or how long it would last.
screen: `HAGIA SOPHIA, JULY 1054.` → `A PAPER ON THE ALTAR.` → `EXCOMMUNICATION, BOTH WAYS.`

segments.voice: Schism comes from the Greek schisma, a tear, a rip in cloth. Jesus uses it in a saying about sewing new cloth onto an old coat: "the rent is made worse." Paul begs the church at Corinth "that there be no divisions among you," the same word. So the Bible itself treats a schism as a wound. What tore in 1054? Two things, mostly. First, authority. The bishop of Rome said he spoke for the whole church, as successor of Peter. The Eastern bishops honored Rome as first among equals, but not as a ruler over them. Second, one word in the creed. Over the centuries, Western churches had added a Latin word, filioque, and the Son, to the line about the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father. The East said nobody had the right to change a creed agreed at a council, and that the change blurred something true about God. Smaller quarrels too: leavened or unleavened bread, beards, fasting days. Historians now say 1054 was less a single day than a long drifting apart: different languages, different empires, and neither side trying very hard to understand the other. The worst blow came in 1204, when Western crusaders sacked Constantinople itself. There were faults on both sides, and churches on both sides now say so. In 1965, Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras formally lifted the excommunications of 1054. They didn't end the split. But they took the paper off the altar.

287.title: The Orthodox Church
287.hook: icons, incense, the Divine Liturgy and becoming like God by grace
287.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians often keep an icon corner at home with a small lamp, cross themselves and kiss the icons when they enter church, and stand through a Divine Liturgy that is sung from start to finish.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was schism: 1054, when East and West tore apart. Your line was the split still aches.

Around the year 987, an old chronicle from Kyiv says, Prince Vladimir sent envoys out to see how different peoples worshiped. Back from Constantinople, from the great church of Hagia Sophia, they could hardly describe it. They said, more or less: we didn't know whether we were in heaven or on earth. We only know that God dwells there among people. The gold, the singing, the incense rising through light from high windows. Soon after, Vladimir was baptized, and with him the people of Kyiv. Step inside an Orthodox church today, Greek, Russian, Romanian, Serbian, Ukrainian, and some visitors still describe what those envoys described. Candles flickering before painted faces. People kissing pictures. Many standing.

Orthodoxy is Greek: orthos, right or straight, and doxa, which means both belief and glory. So: right belief, and right worship, or praise. Orthodox Christians would say you can't separate the two: what you believe is how you pray. The Orthodox Church is a family of self-governing churches, the patriarchates of Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem, and the churches of Russia, Greece, Romania, Serbia and more, sharing one faith and one communion, with no single head. Its main service is the Divine Liturgy, most often the one named for Saint John Chrysostom, sung almost entirely. Icons fill the church: Christ, Mary, the saints. Kissing an icon isn't worshiping wood and paint. A council in 787 said the honor given to an image passes to the one it shows, the way you might kiss a photo of someone you love. And the goal of it all has a surprising name: theosis, becoming like God. It's rooted in a line from Second Peter, that we might be "partakers of the divine nature." Early church fathers went further: God became human so that humans might share God's life. The Orthodox are careful here: not by nature, as if people turn into gods, but by grace, the way iron left in a fire glows with the fire's heat while staying iron. This week's arc: one church, then many; the councils; the ancient churches of Africa and Asia; the road east; 1054; and now worship as heaven on earth.
